description.summary: A bipedal, dog-headed humanoid cryptid reported primarily in the northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, popularized by a 1987 radio prank song by disc jockey Steve Cook of WTCM-FM in Traverse City.
description.full: The Michigan Dogman is a cryptid said to inhabit the forests of the northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, particularly around Wexford, Manistee, and Cross Village. Witnesses describe a roughly seven-foot-tall bipedal creature with a man-like torso, fur, and the head of a dog or wolf, with blue or amber eyes and a vocalization sometimes likened to a human scream. The phenomenon entered popular awareness through 'The Legend', a song that disc jockey Steve Cook recorded as an April Fools' Day prank for WTCM-FM (Traverse City) in 1987. Cook has consistently described the song as fiction; nevertheless it generated more than a hundred reports from listeners and helped seed a regional folklore that was subsequently reinforced by media including MonsterQuest (2010) and the local feature film Dogman (2011). Investigative work by author Linda S. Godfrey, originally focused on Wisconsin's Beast of Bray Road, has since extended to Michigan and the wider Great Lakes region. Mainstream zoology does not recognize the Dogman; reports are typically attributed to misidentification, hoaxes, or the cultural transmission set in motion by Cook's song.

features.description: Wolf- or dog-like head set on a humanoid body
Witnesses report blue or amber eyes, sometimes described as glowing
Howl said to resemble a human cry

physical.morphology: Reports describe a roughly seven-foot bipedal creature with a humanoid (man-like) torso and a canine head.

abilities.description: Howls and screams reported during nocturnal encounters
Said to run upright over short distances

behavior.diet: Unknown; reports do not document feeding behavior
patterns: Reports cluster in northwestern Lower Michigan, particularly Wexford, Manistee, and Cross Village areas
Folklore claims a ten-year cycle linked to years ending in seven
Encounters most often reported at night near forest edges and rural roads

range.description: Reports cluster in the northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan, particularly around the Manistee River and historically Odawa lands; occasional reports extend into other Great Lakes states.

hotspots.name: Wexford County

location.description: Wexford County, northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan

hotspots.notes: Site of the often-cited 1887 lumberjack encounter and the focal area of the post-1987 phenomenon

hotspots.name: Manistee and Cross Village

location.description: Manistee and Cross Village areas, northwestern Michigan

hotspots.notes: Cluster of late-1960s sightings reported in regional press

first_recorded.source: Often-repeated account of two lumberjacks in Wexford County, Michigan

peak_activity_periods.description: Resurgence following Steve Cook's 'The Legend' on WTCM-FM

temporal.seasonal_patterns: No documented seasonal pattern; reports occur year-round.

origins.cultural_roots: Modern Michigan folklore amplified by late-20th-century radio media; situated within a broader Great Lakes context that includes Indigenous Anishinaabe stories of forest beings, though those traditions are distinct from the modern Dogman framing.
origins.earliest_accounts: An 1887 account of two lumberjacks encountering a 'creature with a man's body and dog's head' in Wexford County is the most-cited early report.
origins.folklore_connections: Sits alongside the Wisconsin Beast of Bray Road as a Great Lakes bipedal canine cryptid; broader thematic links to werewolf and loup-garou traditions.

history.modern_era: The contemporary phenomenon is sustained by regional media, podcasting, and books from authors including Linda Godfrey. Cook himself has repeatedly described 'The Legend' as fiction while documenting reports forwarded to him by listeners over the decades.

notable.name: Wexford County lumberjack encounter

location.description: Forest in Wexford County, northwestern Lower Peninsula of Michigan

credibility_factors: Repeated in regional media but no contemporary primary source available

notable.description: Two lumberjacks were said to have encountered a creature with a man's body and the head of a dog in the Wexford County woods. The account is the most-cited 'first' Michigan Dogman incident, though no contemporary primary documentation is on record.

credibility.notes: Foundational folklore item; treat as oral tradition rather than verified case.

sources: Steve Cook / WTCM-FM background materials on 'The Legend'

notable.name: Steve Cook 'The Legend' broadcast
notable.description: Disc jockey Steve Cook aired 'The Legend', a song he wrote as an April Fools' Day prank that wove together fragmentary regional anecdotes into a pseudo-folkloric narrative. Cook has stated the song was made up 'completely from my own imagination as an April Fools' prank'. The song became WTCM-FM's most-requested track and seeded the modern Dogman phenomenon.

credibility.notes: Important not as a sighting but as the cultural origin point of the modern phenomenon.

audio.name: 'The Legend' (Steve Cook, 1987; re-recorded 1997, 2007)
audio.description: Spoken-and-sung folkloric ballad recorded by disc jockey Steve Cook for WTCM-FM as an April Fools' prank, framing the Dogman as a creature appearing on a ten-year cycle.
audio.analysis: Verified as a fictional April Fools' broadcast by its author; treated as the cultural seed of the modern Dogman phenomenon rather than as evidence for the creature.

paranormal.name: Cyclical paranormal entity
paranormal.description: Folkloric framing in 'The Legend' that the creature returns on a ten-year cycle in years ending in seven; treated by some enthusiasts as a literal supernatural pattern.
proponents: Folkloric tradition popularized by Steve Cook's song
evidence_cited: Anecdotal reports clustered around years ending in 7

scientific.name: Undescribed canine cryptid
scientific.description: Speculative framing that reports represent an unrecognized large canine, sometimes proposed in cryptozoological literature alongside the Beast of Bray Road.
evidence_cited: Witness consistency in canine-headed bipedal description across the Great Lakes

skeptical.name: Cultural artifact of the 1987 radio song
skeptical.description: Most reports postdate Steve Cook's 1987 prank song and reflect cultural transmission rather than encounters with a real animal.
proponents: Steve Cook (re: origin of his song)
evidence_cited: Cook's own statements that the song is fiction

skeptical.name: Misidentification of known animals
skeptical.description: Reports may stem from misidentified bears standing on hind legs, large dogs, coyotes, or wolves, particularly at night.
proponents: Skeptical writers on Great Lakes cryptids
evidence_cited: Known black bear behavior of brief bipedal posture
Range overlap with wolves and coyotes in northern Michigan

folklore.beliefs: Dogman folklore in Michigan is largely a late-20th-century invention amplified by regional radio and tourism, distinct from older Indigenous traditions about forest beings.

literature: Books by Linda S. Godfrey treating Great Lakes bipedal canine cryptids

research.ongoing_studies: No ongoing peer-reviewed scientific study; investigation is largely journalistic and folkloric.
